Garment fit, scrotal thermoregulation, and male fertility outcomes: a narrative 
review.

Zleczewski M(1), Clay N(1), Lambert J(2), Stroie F(3).

Author information:
(1)University of Illinois College of Medicine - Peoria, Peoria, IL, USA.
(2)College of Nursing, University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, OH, USA.
(3)Director of Men's Health and Reproductive Urology, Cook County Health, 
Chicago, IL, USA.

BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Scrotal thermoregulation is a recognized feature of 
normal spermatogenesis, with testicular function occurring at temperatures below 
core body temperature. Tight-fitting underwear has been hypothesized to 
influence scrotal temperature, whereas looser garments may allow greater 
ventilation. Public interest in "fertility-friendly" underwear has increased 
despite uncertainty regarding clinical relevance. This narrative review 
synthesizes current literature examining associations between underwear choice, 
particularly garment fit and fabric, and semen parameters and male fertility 
outcomes.
METHODS: A structured literature search of PubMed up to April 20th, 2025 was 
conducted using keywords related to underwear type ("underwear", "boxers", 
"briefs", "undergarments"), scrotal temperature ("scrotal temperature", 
"testicular temperature"), and male fertility ("male fertility", "sperm 
quality", "semen parameters", "sperm concentration", "sperm motility", "sperm 
morphology", "fecundity"). Peer-reviewed human studies published in English 
evaluating underwear fit or fabric in relation to semen parameters, reproductive 
hormones, or fertility outcomes were included. Experimental studies involving 
testicular heat exposure were reviewed to provide physiologic context. Data were 
synthesized qualitatively.
KEY CONTENT AND FINDINGS: Physiologic studies have reported higher scrotal 
temperatures associated with tighter underwear. Observational studies have 
described modest differences in semen parameters between men wearing briefs and 
boxers, while prospective data have not demonstrated differences in pregnancy 
outcomes. Cross-sectional analyses have reported differences in sperm 
concentration and follicle-stimulating hormone levels by underwear type. 
Evidence regarding fabric composition remains limited, and controlled human 
studies comparing materials under typical wearing conditions are lacking.
CONCLUSIONS: Underwear choice has been variably associated with modest 
differences in sperm production parameters, although findings are inconsistent 
and clinical fertility outcomes have not demonstrated clear associations. 
Evidence regarding fabric composition remains limited. In clinical discussions, 
avoidance of excessive scrotal heat exposure may be considered as a general 
measure, while emphasizing that underwear choice alone is unlikely to 
meaningfully influence fertility outcomes for men.
